doc.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024

chapter: Rhythm and the African roots of jazz
title: Learning percussion and the breadth of Latin music
summary: Papo Vazquez had him learn conga and timbale patterns; he came to see Latin music as encyclopedic and feels he graduated to it.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution

blocks.x: hole, you’re not going to be able to. And so I mean you know it was really interesting to me to rediscover the incredible complexity and subtlety of Latin music that you can’t just play. You’re absolutely correct, that you can’t just pick it up. It’s by osmosis. It’s by listening to it. It’s by understanding it. It’s by learning how to play percussion, the great Puerto Rican valve trombonist Papo Vazquez sat me down and actually had me learn the conga patterns and the timbale patterns and all of that is really incredibly important. And you used a beautiful word too because later on after embracing that Cuban-Puerto Rican side of this music I learned about Peruvian music. Festejo, lando, cumbia, vallenato, candombe, I learned that the music that we call “Latin” is encyclopedic. There’s hundreds of varieties of just bomba and plena in Puerto Rico and so in a way I feel like I graduated. And this is not to denigrate jazz, but I feel like I graduated to Latin music.
